issues.legal_issue: Parliament has legislative competence to apply a law providing for eviction of unauthorised occupants to premises owned by a government-controlled statutory corporation.
material_facts: The premises were owned by a statutory corporation established under a Central Act and controlled by the Central Government, rather than being property of the Union itself.
The law provided for eviction of unauthorised occupants from public premises, including premises of such corporations.
The appeal challenged Parliament’s power to apply that law to the premises.
issues.conclusion: The law, as applied to the corporation’s premises, was intra vires Parliament and valid.
issues.legal_principle: Legislative entries are construed by considering a law’s pith and substance and harmonising the entries across the legislative lists. Legislation concerning housing accommodation and control of tenancy in houses and buildings falls within the Concurrent List, including Entries 6, 7 and 13; it is not legislation on the relationship of landlord and tenant in respect of houses and buildings under Entry 18 of the State List. Indu Bhusan Bose v. Rama Sundari Devi and V. Dhanapal Chettiar v. Yesodai Ammal support this approach. The corporation’s separate legal personality means its property is not Union property for purposes of Entry 32 of the Union List; the judgment also relies on Bacha F. Guzdar v. C.I.T., State Trading Corporation of India Ltd. v. C.T.O., A.P. State Road Transport Corporation v. I.T.O., Heavy Engineering Mazdoor Union v. State, Vidarbha Housing Board v. I.T.O. and Western Coalfields Ltd. v. Special Area Development Authority.

predicates.appeal_challenges_parliamentary_legislat: A party in an appeal disputes Parliament’s authority to legislate on the matter at issue.
predicates.eviction_law_applies_to_public_premises: The challenged law provides for eviction of unauthorised occupants from premises treated as public premises.
predicates.premises_belong_to_government_controlled: The premises belong to a statutory corporation controlled by the Central Government, and the corporation has a legal identity distinct from the Union.
predicates.legislation_concerns_tenancy_or_eviction: The legislation concerns housing accommodation or tenancy and eviction relating to buildings.

issues.definition: When an appeal challenges Parliament’s competence over an eviction law applying to public premises of a government-controlled statutory corporation, and the legislation concerns tenancy or eviction of buildings, the rule treats the parliamentary legislation as within legislative competence.

issues.legal_issue: A later parliamentary law on a Concurrent List subject prevails over inconsistent State laws on that subject.
material_facts: The corporation invoked a parliamentary law providing for eviction from public premises.
State laws also provided procedures for eviction from public premises, and the parties disputed which laws governed the eviction.
The parliamentary law was enacted after the relevant State laws.
issues.conclusion: The parliamentary law prevailed over the State laws and was rightly invoked.
issues.legal_principle: Under Article 254(1), a parliamentary law on a Concurrent List subject prevails over a repugnant State law. Article 254(2) did not apply because the State laws were not repugnant to an earlier parliamentary or existing law; its proviso also permits Parliament to enact a later law on the same matter, which prevails even without express amendment or repeal of the State law. The judgment relies on Zaverbhai Amaidas v. State and Hoechst Pharmaceuticals v. State.

predicates.appeal_disputes_which_eviction_law_appli: A party in an appeal disputes which of competing eviction laws governs the proceeding.
predicates.parliamentary_and_state_laws_cover_the_s: A parliamentary law and State laws address the same subject within the Concurrent List.
predicates.parliamentary_law_was_enacted_after_stat: The parliamentary law was enacted after the relevant State laws.

issues.definition: When an appeal concerns which law governs and parliamentary and State laws cover the same Concurrent List subject, a later parliamentary law prevails over the State law.

issues.legal_issue: Appointing an officer of a public authority that owns or controls the premises as the officer responsible for eviction proceedings does not, by itself, violate equality guarantees.
material_facts: A provision of the eviction law allowed an officer of the corporation owning the premises to act as the eviction officer.
The law provided an appeal from the eviction officer’s order to an independent judicial officer.
The appellants challenged the officer’s appointment as discriminatory.
issues.conclusion: The challenge to the appointment under the equality guarantee had no substance.
issues.legal_principle: The judgment considered Article 14 and held that an officer or appointee of the government, statutory authority or corporation may implement the eviction law; the officer’s employment by that authority does not, by itself, establish personal bias. The availability of an appeal to an independent judicial officer also supported the conclusion that the arrangement was not invalid.

predicates.appeal_challenges_eviction_officer_appoi: A party in an appeal challenges the appointment or role of the officer conducting eviction proceedings.
predicates.officer_is_employed_by_authority_respons: The officer is employed by the government, statutory authority or corporation responsible for the premises.
predicates.independent_judicial_appeal_is_available: The law provides an appeal from the officer’s order to an independent judicial officer.

issues.definition: When an appeal challenges an eviction officer who is employed by the authority responsible for the premises, the availability of an independent judicial appeal means that the appointment does not, by itself, violate equality.
